title: Computer Networking Fundamentals
summary: Understand networks, TCP/IP layers, IP addressing and subnetting, Wi-Fi and speed, troubleshooting and basic network security, with calculations.
audience: Students, IT support beginners and anyone preparing for entry-level networking certificates

body.p: A computer network connects devices so that they can share data and resources. Your phone, laptop, printer, school server and the websites you visit are all on networks. Networks come in sizes. A PAN connects personal devices over a few metres. A LAN covers a home, school or office. A MAN covers a city. A WAN covers large areas, and the internet is a network of networks.

list: Hosts or end devices: computers, phones, servers.
Network interface card (NIC): connects a device, wired or wireless.
Switch: connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the right port.
Router: connects different networks and sends packets between them, such as your home network and the internet.
Access point: lets wireless devices join a wired network.
Cables and wireless links: copper, fibre and radio.

body.p: In a client-server model, clients request services from servers, such as a browser requesting a web page. In peer-to-peer sharing, devices share directly with each other.

body.tip: Draw your home network on paper: the modem or router, each device and how it connects. It makes later lessons easier.

body.p: Data on a network follows agreed rules called protocols. To manage this complexity, we describe networking in layers. The simplified TCP/IP model has four layers.

list: Application: services used by programs, such as HTTP for web pages, SMTP for mail and DNS for names.
Transport: moves data between programs. TCP is reliable and ordered. UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery, and is used for video calls and games.
Internet: addressing and routing with IP.
Link: delivery on the local network, including Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

steps: You type a web address. DNS translates the name into an IP address.
Your browser opens a TCP connection to the server.
The browser sends an HTTP request.
The server replies with the page in many small packets.
Your device reassembles the packets in order and displays the page.

body.p: Each packet has a header with source and destination addresses. Routers use these to forward packets hop by hop.

Every device on an IP network needs an address. An IPv4 address has 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.10. Each number is 8 bits. For example, 192 in binary is 11000000 and 168 is 10101000.

A subnet mask or prefix length shows which bits identify the network and which identify the host. In 192.168.1.0/24, the first 24 bits are the network, leaving 8 bits for hosts: 2^8 = 256 addresses. Two are reserved, the network address and the broadcast address, so 254 can be given to devices. With /26, there are 6 host bits, so 2^6 = 64 addresses and 62 usable.
Splitting 192.168.1.0/24 into /26 subnets gives four subnets of 64 addresses: .0 to .63, .64 to .127, .128 to .191 and .192 to .255.

list: Private ranges such as 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x and 172.16 to 172.31 are used inside homes and organisations. Network address translation (NAT) lets many private devices share one public address.
IPv6 uses 128 bits to give a vastly larger address space as IPv4 addresses run out.
DHCP automatically gives devices their address settings, and DNS translates names to addresses.

body.p: Wi-Fi uses radio waves. Signal weakens with distance and obstacles such as thick walls. Place your router in a central, open spot. Use strong security (WPA2 or WPA3) with a long, unique password, and change the default router login.

Bandwidth is how much data a link can carry per second, usually in megabits per second (Mbps). There are 8 bits in a byte, so file sizes in megabytes are multiplied by 8 to compare with Mbps. A 100 MB file at 50 Mbps needs 100 x 8 = 800 megabits, divided by 50 Mbps, which gives 16 seconds in ideal conditions. Real speeds are lower because of overheads and sharing. Latency is the delay for data to travel and matters for calls and games.

steps: Check the problem is not just one device or one website.
Check cables, power and Wi-Fi status.
Restart the device and then the router.
Check that the device has a valid IP address.
Use ping to test connection to the router, then to a website.
If only names fail, suspect DNS. If nothing works, contact the provider.

body.p: Security protects confidentiality (only the right people can read data), integrity (data is not altered) and availability (services work when needed).

list: Firewalls filter traffic according to rules.
Encryption scrambles data so that eavesdroppers cannot read it. HTTPS uses it for websites, and a VPN uses it for traffic between your device and a network.
Strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication.
Software and firmware updates to fix known weaknesses.
Network segmentation, for example a guest Wi-Fi separate from the school's staff network.
Backups kept offline or away from the main system.
Phishing and social engineering.
Malware and ransomware.
Denial of service attacks that flood a service.
Weak or default passwords.
Unsecured public Wi-Fi.

body.p: Only test or scan networks that you own or have written permission to test. Unauthorised access is a crime in most countries.

The best way to learn networking is to build small networks. Free tools such as packet simulators let you drag routers, switches and computers and practise configuration without equipment. At home you can use commands such as ipconfig or ip addr to see your address, ping to test reachability and tracert or traceroute to see the path packets take.

list: Draw a plan for a small office with 20 computers, a printer and Wi-Fi, and choose a subnet size that allows growth.
Set up a secure guest Wi-Fi.
Document your home network: devices, addresses and passwords stored safely.

body.p: Networking opens roles such as help desk technician, network technician, network administrator, systems engineer, security analyst and cloud engineer. Industry certificates, for example entry-level networking and security certifications from recognised vendors and bodies, help employers see your skills. Check what employers in your country ask for.

body.tip: Keep notes of every problem you solve and how you solved it. This becomes your troubleshooting playbook and a good talking point in interviews.

quiz.q: Which device connects different networks and forwards packets between them?
Which network type usually covers a single school or office?
Which transport protocol is reliable and ordered?
How many bits does an IPv4 address have?
How many usable host addresses are in a /24 network?
How many usable host addresses are in a /26 network?
Which of these is a private IPv4 range?
How long does a 100 MB file take at 50 Mbps, ideally?
Which setting best secures a home Wi-Fi?
options: WPA2 or WPA3 with a long unique password
Hiding the router in a cupboard

quiz.q: Which tool tests whether a device can reach another?
Which is allowed when scanning a network?
options: Only networks you own or have written permission to test
